title: Base-10 Digit Sum via Nat.digits
content: The digit sum is defined as the sum of the list returned by Nat.digits 10 n. Lean 4's Nat.digits decomposes a natural number into its base-b digit representation as a list (least significant digit first). For example, Nat.digits 10 1234 = [4, 3, 2, 1]. The .sum method then adds all elements. This definition is mathematically equivalent to $\sum_{k=0}^{\lfloor \log_{10} n \rfloor} a_k$ where $n = \sum a_k \cdot 10^k$, but the list-based formulation makes inductive reasoning natural in Lean.
mathContext: $\text{digitSum}(n) = \sum_{i} a_i$ where $n = \sum_i a_i \cdot 10^i$ is the base-10 representation. Equivalently, $\text{digitSum} = \text{List.sum} \circ (\text{Nat.digits}\ 10)$.

title: Weak Bound: digitSum(n) ≤ n by Strong Recursion
content: The proof that the digit sum never exceeds the number itself uses Nat.strongRecOn (well-founded recursion on ℕ). The base case handles n < 10 by exhaustive computation (interval_cases + native_decide). For n ≥ 10, the key step uses Nat.digits_def' to decompose the digit list as n%10 :: digits(n/10), giving digitSum(n) = n%10 + digitSum(n/10). The inductive hypothesis applies to n/10 < n, yielding digitSum(n/10) ≤ n/10, and omega closes the gap: n%10 + n/10 ≤ n follows from the Euclidean division identity n = 10·(n/10) + n%10.
mathContext: $\text{digitSum}(n) = (n \bmod 10) + \text{digitSum}(\lfloor n/10 \rfloor) \leq (n \bmod 10) + \lfloor n/10 \rfloor \leq n$. The last step uses $n = 10 \lfloor n/10 \rfloor + (n \bmod 10) \geq \lfloor n/10 \rfloor + (n \bmod 10)$.

title: Strict Decrease: digitSum(n) < n for n ≥ 10
content: This is the engine of the termination argument. For n ≥ 10, the digit sum is strictly less than n. The proof unfolds digitSum, applies Nat.digits_def' to get the cons structure, then uses the weak bound digitSum_le_self on n/10 to obtain digitSum(n) ≤ n%10 + n/10. The strict inequality n%10 + n/10 < n holds because n/10 < n for n ≥ 10 (since n has at least two digits, the leading digits contribute a multiplicative factor ≥ 10). This is the key fact that makes the iteration well-founded: each step strictly reduces the argument until we reach a single digit.
mathContext: For $n \geq 10$: $\text{digitSum}(n) = (n \bmod 10) + \text{digitSum}(\lfloor n/10 \rfloor) \leq (n \bmod 10) + \lfloor n/10 \rfloor < n$. The strict inequality comes from $10 \cdot \lfloor n/10 \rfloor \leq n$, so $\lfloor n/10 \rfloor \leq n/10 < n$ when $n \geq 10$.

title: Casting Out Nines: digitSum(n) ≡ n (mod 9)
content: This one-line proof encapsulates one of the oldest computational tricks in mathematics. The digit sum preserves the residue mod 9 because 10 ≡ 1 (mod 9), so each positional weight 10^k ≡ 1^k = 1 (mod 9). The proof delegates entirely to Mathlib's Nat.modEq_digits_sum, which proves the general statement: if base ≡ 1 (mod d), then (digits base n).sum ≡ n (mod d). The native_decide call verifies 10 % 9 = 1. This technique, known since at least the 12th century via Fibonacci's Liber Abaci, is the algebraic core that identifies the digital root.
mathContext: $10 \equiv 1 \pmod{9}$ implies $10^k \equiv 1 \pmod{9}$ for all $k$. Therefore $n = \sum a_k \cdot 10^k \equiv \sum a_k \pmod{9}$, i.e., $\text{digitSum}(n) \equiv n \pmod{9}$.

title: Base Cases: digitSum at 0 and Single Digits
content: Two base case lemmas establish the boundary behavior. digitSum_zero shows that the empty digit list sums to 0 (by simp). digitSum_single shows digitSum is the identity on {0, ..., 9} — these are already single digits, so the digit list is [n] and its sum is n. The proof uses interval_cases to enumerate all 10 possibilities and native_decide for each. These facts are crucial for the convergence proof: they establish that single digits are fixed points of the iteration.
mathContext: $\text{digitSum}(0) = 0$ and $\text{digitSum}(n) = n$ for $0 \leq n < 10$. Single digits are fixed points of the digit sum operation.

title: Positivity Gap: digitSum(n) > 0 for n > 0
content: This lemma has the file's only sorry, for the case n ≥ 10. The strategy is sound: the leading digit (last element of Nat.digits 10 n, since digits are stored LSB-first) is nonzero by Nat.getLast_digit_ne_zero, so the sum of the digit list is at least 1. The gap is a missing API lemma: List.single_le_sum (or List.getLast_le_sum), which says that any element of a nonneg list is ≤ the list's sum. The n < 10 case is handled by exhaustive computation. This sorry is non-blocking for the main theorem since iterDigitSum_pos (which depends on it) is only used in the n%9 = 0 branch of the convergence proof.
mathContext: For $n \geq 10$: $\text{digits}_{10}(n)$ has $\geq 2$ elements, and the leading digit $a_{\lfloor \log_{10} n \rfloor} \neq 0$ by definition. So $\text{digitSum}(n) \geq a_{\lfloor \log_{10} n \rfloor} \geq 1 > 0$.

title: Termination by Strong Induction
content: The termination theorem proves that iterating digitSum on any n eventually produces a value < 10. The proof is a textbook application of strong induction with a decreasing measure: for n < 10 the iteration terminates immediately (k = 0); for n ≥ 10, digitSum_lt_of_ge_ten gives digitSum(n) < n, so the inductive hypothesis applies to digitSum(n), yielding k' with (digitSum^[k'])(digitSum(n)) < 10, and k = k'+1 works. The iterate is unfolded via Function.iterate_succ and Function.comp. This pattern — strict decrease + strong induction — is the canonical approach for termination of numeric iterations in Lean 4.
mathContext: Define $a_0 = n$, $a_{k+1} = \text{digitSum}(a_k)$. Since $a_{k+1} < a_k$ whenever $a_k \geq 10$, the sequence $(a_k)$ is eventually $< 10$. Formally: $\exists k,\, a_k < 10$, proved by strong induction on $n$.

title: Mod 9 Loop Invariant Across All Iterations
content: This theorem establishes that the mod 9 residue class is preserved through every iteration step: (digitSum^[k])(n) ≡ n (mod 9) for all k. The proof is a clean induction on k. The base case is trivial (zero iterations preserve everything). The inductive step uses digitSum_modEq_9 (single-step preservation) composed with the IH via ModEq.trans. The Function.iterate_succ' variant unfolds the k+1 case as digitSum applied after k iterations. This invariant is the algebraic backbone of the convergence proof: it pins down the terminal single-digit value.
mathContext: $\text{digitSum}^{[k]}(n) \equiv n \pmod{9}$ for all $k \in \mathbb{N}$. Proof by induction: $\text{digitSum}^{[k+1]}(n) = \text{digitSum}(\text{digitSum}^{[k]}(n)) \equiv \text{digitSum}^{[k]}(n) \equiv n \pmod{9}$.

title: Main Theorem: Iterated Digit Sum Converges to digitalRoot
content: The crown jewel of the formalization. Starting from any n, there exists k such that (digitSum^[k])(n) = digitalRoot(n). The proof obtains the termination index k and sets m = (digitSum^[k])(n), which satisfies m < 10 and m ≡ n (mod 9). Then it unfolds the digitalRoot definition and handles three cases: (1) n = 0: all iterates of 0 are 0, matching digitalRoot(0) = 0. (2) n > 0 with 9 | n: m is a positive single digit with m ≡ 0 (mod 9), so m = 9 = digitalRoot(n). (3) n > 0 with 9 ∤ n: m is a single digit with m % 9 = n % 9 ≠ 0, so m = n % 9 = digitalRoot(n). Each case is closed by interval_cases m <;> omega, which enumerates m ∈ {0,...,9} and checks the modular constraint.
mathContext: $\forall n \in \mathbb{N},\, \exists k \in \mathbb{N}: \text{digitSum}^{[k]}(n) = \text{digitalRoot}(n)$. The terminal value $m < 10$ with $m \equiv n \pmod{9}$ is unique: $m = 0$ if $n = 0$; $m = 9$ if $9 \mid n > 0$; $m = n \bmod 9$ otherwise.

title: Fixed Point Properties of digitalRoot
content: Two corollaries establish that the digital root is a fixed point of digit summation. iterDigitSum_terminal_fixed shows that the terminal iterate satisfies digitSum(m) = m (using digitSum_single since m < 10). digitalRoot_is_fixed_point directly proves digitSum(digitalRoot(n)) = digitalRoot(n) by noting digitalRoot(n) ≤ 9 (from digitalRoot_le_9 in the parent file), so it's a single digit. These facts confirm that the digital root is not just the limit of the iteration, but a genuine absorbing state: once reached, the iteration stays there forever.
mathContext: $\text{digitSum}(\text{digitalRoot}(n)) = \text{digitalRoot}(n)$ for all $n$. Since $\text{digitalRoot}(n) < 10$, it is a single digit, and single digits are fixed points of $\text{digitSum}$.

title: Uniqueness: digitalRoot Is the Only Single-Digit Fixed Point mod 9
content: The uniqueness theorem provides a complete characterization: any m satisfying (1) m < 10, (2) m ≡ n (mod 9), and (3) m = 0 iff n = 0 must equal digitalRoot(n). This is stronger than convergence alone — it says the digital root is the unique such value. The proof mirrors the convergence argument's case analysis: unfold digitalRoot, split on n = 0 and n % 9 = 0, and close each case with interval_cases m <;> omega. The zero-status hypothesis (3) is needed to distinguish digitalRoot(0) = 0 from digitalRoot(9) = 9, since both are single digits with residue 0 mod 9.
mathContext: If $m < 10$, $m \equiv n \pmod{9}$, and $m = 0 \iff n = 0$, then $m = \text{digitalRoot}(n)$. This characterizes the digital root uniquely among single digits.
